title: What Renters, Google and AI Tools Need to Find on an Apartment Community Website: A Checklist
seoTitle: Apartment Website Checklist for Renters, Google and AI
seoDescription: A checklist of what an apartment community website must show renters, Google and AI tools: pricing and fees, floor plans, policies, location, tours and access.
excerpt: Renters, Google and AI tools all need the same facts from your site: price and fees, floor plans, policies and how to tour, in plain text that matches everywhere else.
imageAlt: Young woman sitting by a bright window on a sofa, looking at a tablet and holding a stylus
imageIdea: Real photo of a renter browsing on a tablet or phone at home in daylight, screen not readable, no visible brand logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
An apartment community website needs to state the facts renters use to decide, in plain text on pages anyone can open: price and fees, floor plans and availability, pet and parking rules, location and how to tour. Google and AI tools need those same facts, readable and consistent with your Google Business Profile and listings.

We have written about why AI tools struggle to read many property websites. This post is the checklist we use when we review one.

Why does the website still matter if renters start on listing sites?

Because it is the one source you fully control. Listing sites, Google and AI tools summarize what they find, and when your site is vague or out of date, those summaries are too.

In an Apartments.com survey reported by the National Apartment Association, 87% of more than 15,000 adults planning to rent had no specific property in mind when they started, and 85% said they use or plan to use a site like Apartments.com. Apartments.com ran the survey. Even so, the pattern is clear: renters compare before they know your name, and your site is where they check the details.

What pricing and fee information should the site show?

Show starting rent by floor plan, every required monthly fee, one time fees and deposits, all on a page that does not require an application. Renters treat surprise fees as a reason to leave, and some states regulate how rental prices are advertised.

Colorado's HB25-1090, for example, requires advertised prices to include mandatory fees as a single total shown more prominently than other pricing information. Other states have their own rules, so have counsel confirm what applies where you operate. Whatever the law, a clear fee table is easier for a renter, Google and an AI tool to read than a footnote.

What should floor plan and availability pages include?

Each floor plan should list bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, starting price, available dates and real photos or a tour of that plan. Availability that is weeks out of date costs trust fast. The same NAA report says that for half of respondents, a listing without photos of the specific unit is a deal breaker.

If your availability comes from a feed or widget, open the page on a phone and make sure the plan names, prices and dates actually appear as text. A grid that only loads after several clicks, or only inside an image, is hard for search engines and AI tools to use.

What policies do renters look for?

Pets, parking, lease terms, utilities and application requirements. These are the questions leasing teams answer by phone every day, and each one belongs on the site in a sentence or a short table.

For pets, list species, any breed or weight rules, pet rent, fees and deposits. Have your legal or compliance contact review any wording about assistance animals before it goes live. For parking, say what is included, what costs extra and whether there is a waitlist. For applications, state the criteria you already apply, written the same way for every applicant.

What do Google and AI tools need from the site?

They need pages that can be crawled and indexed, with the important facts in text. Google says a page must be indexed and eligible to show a snippet to appear as a supporting link in its AI Overviews and AI Mode, and that no special AI text files or special structured data are required for that.

Consistency matters too. Google says complete and accurate information helps it match your business with the right searches. If your site lists one pet fee, your Google Business Profile lists another and a listing site shows a third, renters and AI tools are left to guess. Our post on Google Business Profile and AI search covers the profile side.

What accessibility basics should the site cover?

Make sure people using screen readers, keyboards or captions can find units, prices and contact options. The Department of Justice's guidance on web accessibility and the ADA says businesses open to the public should make their websites accessible, and points to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines as a helpful reference. It does not set one required technical standard for businesses, so ask your web vendor which standard they build to.

Practical checks: alt text on photos, readable color contrast, captions on video tours, forms that work without a mouse and a phone number in text, not only in an image.

What is the full checklist?

Here is the list we work through. Each item should be visible as text on a page that loads without a login or an application.

  • Community name, street address and phone number, matching your Google Business Profile
  • Office hours and self guided tour hours, updated for holidays
  • Starting rent by floor plan, with the date it was last updated
  • A fee table: required monthly fees, one time fees, deposits
  • Floor plans with bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage and real photos
  • Availability dates that match your property management system
  • Pet policy, parking, utilities and lease term options
  • Application criteria and steps, written the same for every applicant
  • Current specials with their terms and end date
  • Neighborhood facts you can verify, such as distances to major employers or transit
  • How to book a tour, in one or two clicks
  • The Equal Housing Opportunity statement or logo your compliance team uses
  • Accessibility basics: alt text, captions, keyboard friendly forms

Checking that your site, profile and AI answers agree is part of what we track every week in LocalLift.

Questions we hear

Should rent prices be on our apartment website?

Yes, at least starting rent by floor plan, with required fees shown clearly. Some states, including Colorado, regulate how rental prices and mandatory fees are advertised, so confirm the rules where you operate.

Do we need special schema or an AI file for ChatGPT or Google AI Overviews?

Google says no special AI text files or special structured data are needed to appear in its AI features. The page must be indexed and eligible to show a snippet, and the facts should be in readable text.

Why does our availability widget matter for search?

If prices and dates only load inside a widget or image, search engines and AI tools may not read them. Check that the key facts appear as text on the page.

Does the ADA apply to apartment websites?

The Department of Justice says businesses open to the public should make their websites accessible and points to WCAG as a reference. Ask counsel how it applies to your communities.

How often should we review the website?

Check prices, fees, specials and availability weekly, and review the full checklist each quarter or whenever a policy changes.
